crates.name: apsis-core
crates.summary: Shared foundation types for the ApsisRS workspace: a general purpose error type, result aliases, physical constants, and the unit marker trait. This crate sits at the bottom of the dependency graph. It has no dependency on any other ApsisRS crate, so every other crate may use it. Three concerns live here: - [`Error`] and [`Result`] are a general purpose error carrying a coarse [`ErrorKind`]. They exist so that a function whose failure has no interesting structure can report it without inventing a type, and so that the workspace has a shape to fall back on. They are deliberately *not* the error type of the layers: a layer with a domain specific failure defines its own `Error` and `ErrorKind`, whose variants name the concrete conditions a caller would want to match on. See `docs/design/errors.md` for why, and for the conventions the domain errors follow. - [`constant`] holds physical and astronomical constants expressed in SI units. - [`Quantity`] marks newtypes that carry a physical unit, so generic code can accept any quantity and still recover its unit type.

crates.name: apsis-units
crates.summary: Strongly typed newtypes for physical quantities. Each quantity is a newtype over `f64` that carries its unit in the type system, so a length cannot be passed where a duration is expected. Units of the same dimension convert through [`Quantity::to_unit`], and each unit also offers direct conversions for the common cases. A newtype implements both [`Unit`] and [`Quantity`], with its own type as the associated unit. For example [`Meters`] is a [`Length`](dimension::Length) unit and a quantity whose unit is itself. The dimensions covered here are length, time, frequency, angle, and thermodynamic temperature. Temperature is the only affine scale in the set, so Celsius is handled by explicit methods on [`Kelvin`] rather than by the linear [`Unit`] conversion factor. ``` use apsis_core::Quantity; use apsis_units::{Kilometers, Meters}; let distance = Meters::new(2_500.0); let in_kilometers: Kilometers = distance.to_unit(); assert!((in_kilometers.value() - 2.5).abs() < 1e-12); ```

crates.name: apsis-math
crates.summary: Dependency-free linear algebra for the ApsisRS workspace. The crate provides three types: - [`Vec3`], a three component column vector over `f64` - [`Quat`], a unit quaternion used for rotations - [`Mat3`], a three by three matrix stored in column-major order The types are plain data with no interior invariants beyond those documented on each method, so their fields are public and a value can be built by struct literal expression. Operations that are mathematically undefined for some inputs, such as normalizing the zero vector, return [`Option`] instead of panicking or producing a non-finite result. All rotations use the right-hand rule about the given axis, and all angles are in radians. Angles are not wrapped on input; methods that require a canonical range document that requirement. ``` use apsis_math::Vec3; let x = Vec3::new(1.0, 0.0, 0.0); let y = Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0); let z = x.cross(y); assert_eq!(z, Vec3::new(0.0, 0.0, 1.0)); ```

items.name: for_each_index
items.signature: pub fn for_each_index<F>(len: usize, operation: F) where F: Fn(usize) + Sync, {
items.doc:
Runs a closure once for each index of a range, spread over several threads.

The range is split into one contiguous chunk per thread and each thread
runs the closure for the indices in its chunk. The closure may be called
from any thread, so it must be `Send` and `Sync`; anything it captures is
shared rather than copied. The call returns only after every thread has
finished, so the data the closure wrote is safe to read afterwards.

The closure is handed the index rather than the element, which keeps the
signature independent of the collection: the caller reads the input and
writes the output itself, and the two never overlap.

# Panics

If the closure panics, the panic is resumed on the calling thread after
the other threads have been joined, so a failure surfaces at the call
rather than in a detached thread.

items.doc:
Collects one value for each index of a range, spread over several threads.

This is [`for_each_index`] for the common case where the result of the
work is a value rather than a write into a shared array. The output is
returned in index order regardless of which thread produced which element,
so it does not depend on the scheduling.

The closure is handed the index and returns the value for that index. As
with [`for_each_index`], it may run on any thread, so captured data must be
`Sync`.

vector applies `b` first, then `a`.

crates.name: apsis-macros
crates.summary: Macros that support the ApsisRS workspace. This crate currently defines no macros. It exists so that the workspace has a single place for macro definitions if a need arises, and so that adding one later does not require a new crate. The decision to leave it empty follows from what the workspace actually needs. Rust's built in `macro_rules!` can already do everything the foundation layer requires: - Substituting a type and a literal to build a quantity, as `quantity!(Meters, 1.5)`. - Dispatching on a trailing token to accept a unit suffix, as `to_meters!(2.5 km)`. Both forms are demonstrated by the tests in `tests/probe.rs`. They can be written directly in the crate that uses them, so no shared macro crate is needed. Two limits are worth recording, because they explain why a macro based unit system is not provided: - A `macro_rules!` macro cannot be generic over a unit suffix that is not an identifier. `1.5 m` and `1.5 km` are accepted by separate rules, so the macro must enumerate every suffix it supports. The unit newtypes in `apsis-units` already give compile time unit safety without that list, so the macro would add surface area without adding checking. - A declarative macro cannot inspect the value of its arguments, so it cannot fold a unit conversion at compile time beyond what constant evaluation already does. A literal such as `2.5 * 1000.0` is folded by the compiler anyway. If the workspace later needs macros that generate items, such as deriving a set of conversions from one definition, that is the point at which this crate should gain its first macro.

crates.name: apsis-time
crates.summary: Time scales, epochs, and calendar conversions. This crate provides the time model used by the rest of the workspace. An [`Epoch`] is an instant stored as a Modified Julian Date on the International Atomic Time scale, and [`TimeScale`] names the scale a number is expressed in. Storing a single uniform scale makes the arithmetic exact: the difference between two epochs is the elapsed SI time between them, independent of the scales they were created in. UTC is not uniform, because leap seconds are inserted to keep it near the rotation of the Earth, so UTC conversions are routed through the table in `apsis-leap`. ``` use apsis_time::{Calendar, Epoch, TimeScale}; // Build an instant from a UTC calendar date and read it back. let calendar = Calendar::from_ymd(2024, 6, 15); let epoch = Epoch::from_calendar(calendar, TimeScale::Utc).expect("covered by the leap table"); let back = epoch.calendar(TimeScale::Utc).expect("covered by the leap table"); assert_eq!(back.year, 2024); assert_eq!(back.month, 6); assert_eq!(back.day, 15); ``` Sources: - Julian date and Modified Julian date conventions: IAU, as described in the *Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac*. - Terrestrial Time offset from TAI: IAU 2000 Resolution B1.9. - Leap seconds: IERS Bulletin C, embedded by `apsis-leap`. - Calendar algorithms: Howard Hinnant, *chrono-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms*, 2015.

crates.name: apsis-leap
crates.summary: Embedded leap second table for the UTC time scale. Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) is kept within 0.9 s of UT1 by inserting or removing leap seconds. Because UTC is not a uniform time scale, converting between UTC and the uniform scales TAI, TT, and GPS requires the offset `TAI - UTC` in force at the instant of interest. This crate embeds that offset as a compile time table and answers queries against it. Dates are handled as Modified Julian Date (MJD), which is the Julian Date minus 2 400 000.5. An MJD is a count of days since 1858-11-17T00:00:00, so it carries no time scale of its own; the caller states the scale by choosing which function to call. The table begins at 1972-01-01, when UTC adopted the current integer second offset scheme. Offsets before that date were fractional and followed a different rule, so queries earlier than the first entry return `None` rather than a misleading value. Source: IERS Bulletin C, which announces leap seconds after confirmation by the International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service. The most recent entry in this table is the leap second of 2017-01-01; no leap second has been announced since. ``` use apsis_leap::{tai_minus_utc_at_mjd, LEAP_SECONDS}; // The last entry in the embedded table fixes the current offset. let last = LEAP_SECONDS.last().expect("table is not empty"); assert_eq!(last.tai_minus_utc, 37.0); assert_eq!(tai_minus_utc_at_mjd(60_000.0), Some(37.0)); ```

crates.name: apsis-coord
crates.summary: Coordinate frames and the transformations between them. This crate defines positions that carry their reference frame in the type, so a position expressed in one frame cannot be passed where another is expected. The two frames are the Earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame and the Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF) frame. Three position representations are offered: - [`Eci`], an inertial Cartesian position in meters - [`Ecef`], an Earth-fixed Cartesian position in meters - [`Geodetic`], a latitude, longitude, and height above the WGS 84 ellipsoid The transformation between [`Eci`] and [`Ecef`] is the rotation defined by the Earth Rotation Angle, which `apsis-frames` computes. The transformation between [`Ecef`] and [`Geodetic`] uses the WGS 84 ellipsoid from `apsis-geodesy`. ``` use apsis_coord::{Ecef, Eci, Geodetic, WGS84}; use apsis_frames::EarthRotationAngle; use apsis_math::Vec3; // A station on the equator at zero longitude. let station = Geodetic::new(0.0, 0.0, 0.0); let fixed = station.to_ecef(); assert!((fixed.vector().x - WGS84.semi_major_axis()).abs() < 1e-6); // Rotating it into the inertial frame preserves its length. let inertial = fixed.to_eci(EarthRotationAngle::from_ut1_days(0.0)); assert!((inertial.vector().norm() - fixed.vector().norm()).abs() < 1e-6); let _ = Eci::new(Vec3::X); ``` Sources: - Earth Rotation Angle: *IERS Conventions (2010)*, equation 8.32, as implemented by `apsis-frames`. - Geodetic conversions and the WGS 84 ellipsoid: NIMA TR8350.2, third edition, 2000, as implemented by `apsis-geodesy`.

crates.summary: Reference ellipsoids and geodetic computations. A geodetic position is written as latitude, longitude, and height above an ellipsoid. Latitude here is always geodetic, the angle between the ellipsoid normal and the equatorial plane, not geocentric. The two differ by up to about 0.19 degrees at mid latitudes, so the distinction matters for pointing and ranging. [`WGS84`] is the ellipsoid used by GPS and by almost all satellite work. Its defining parameters are the semi-major axis and the inverse flattening; every other quantity is derived from those two, so the derived values agree with the ones published in the standard to the precision of the defining parameters. Source: National Imagery and Mapping Agency, *Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984*, Technical Report TR8350.2, third edition, 2000. ``` use apsis_geodesy::{Geodetic, WGS84}; // The equator has zero height and a radius equal to the semi-major axis. let point = Geodetic::new(0.0, 0.0, 0.0); let cartesian = point.to_cartesian(WGS84); assert!((cartesian.norm() - WGS84.semi_major_axis()).abs() < 1e-9); ```

items.signature: pub fn to_cartesian(self, ellipsoid: Ellipsoid) -> Vec3 {
items.doc:

The frame has its third axis along the ellipsoid's minor axis through
the north pole, its first axis through the intersection of the
equator and the prime meridian, and its second axis completing a
right-handed set. The result is in meters.

The closed form is

```text
N = a / sqrt(1 - e^2 sin^2(lat))
x = (N + h) cos(lat) cos(lon)
y = (N + h) cos(lat) sin(lon)
z = (N (1 - e^2) + h) sin(lat)
```

where `N` is the prime vertical radius of curvature. This form is
exact everywhere, including at the poles, where the cosine factors
vanish.

crates.name: apsis-frames
crates.summary: Reference frame definitions and the rotation between the inertial and Earth-fixed frames. A reference frame fixes the orientation and origin that a vector is expressed relative to. This crate names the two frames used for near-Earth work and computes the rotation between them. Concrete position types that carry a frame are defined in `apsis-coord`; this crate works with the rotation matrix and the angle that defines it. The inertial frame is the Earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame aligned with the mean equator and equinox of J2000.0. Its axes are fixed in inertial space, so an orbit propagated in it is not affected by the rotation of the Earth. The rotating frame is the Earth-centered Earth-fixed (ECEF) frame. Its third axis is the Earth's rotation axis and its first axis follows the prime meridian, so a point fixed to the ground has constant coordinates in it. The two are related by a rotation of [`EarthRotationAngle`] about the common third axis. This crate models the Earth's rotation with the Earth Rotation Angle, which is a function of UT1 only. It does not apply precession or nutation, because an angle accurate to a few hundredths of a degree is sufficient for pointing and coverage work and the full model needs the orientation of the celestial pole, which is a separate computation. Source: the Earth Rotation Angle expression is from the International Astronomical Union, as given in the *IERS Conventions (2010)*, equation 8.32. ``` use apsis_frames::{EarthRotationAngle, rotation_eci_to_ecef}; // The angle advances by roughly 360.9856 degrees per day. let first = EarthRotationAngle::from_ut1_days(0.0); let second = EarthRotationAngle::from_ut1_days(1.0); let advance = (second.radians() - first.radians()).to_degrees(); assert!((advance - 360.985_612_288_088).abs() < 1e-6); // The rotation is ready to apply to a vector. let _ = rotation_eci_to_ecef(first); ```

crates.name: apsis-tle
crates.summary: Parsing of two-line element sets. A two-line element set (TLE) describes a satellite orbit in the form used by the North American Aerospace Defense Command and distributed by Space-Track. The name of the satellite is carried on an optional first line, and the two following lines carry the orbital data. The format is fixed width. Every field occupies a fixed range of columns and the checksum of each line is the sum of its digits modulo ten, where a minus sign counts as one. This crate parses a TLE into structured fields and verifies the line checksums and the matching element set number. It does not interpret the fields; the mean elements and their units are the concern of `apsis-sgp4`. Column positions are one based, matching the documentation of the format. Two conventions from the format are worth stating explicitly, because they are easy to misread: - An exponent field is written as a signed single digit followed by the magnitude. For example ` 12345-3` means `0.12345e-3`, not `12345e-3`. - An assumed decimal point is written without a decimal point. For example the eccentricity field `0006703` means `0.0006703`. Source: the field layout follows the format description published by CelesTrak, *FAQs: Two-Line Element Set Format*, which documents the columns defined by the original NORAD specification. The checksum rule is the one stated there and used by Space-Track. ``` use apsis_tle::TwoLineElement; let text = concat!( "1 25544U 98067A 08264.51782528 -.00002182 00000-0 -11606-4 0 2927\r\n", "2 25544 51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.72125391563537\r\n", ); let element = TwoLineElement::parse(text).expect("sample is well formed"); assert_eq!(element.satellite_number, 25544); assert!((element.eccentricity - 0.0006703).abs() < 1e-12); ```

crates.name: apsis-sgp4
crates.summary: The SGP4 and SDP4 analytical orbit propagator. The propagator takes the mean orbital elements of a two-line element set and returns the position and velocity of the satellite at a requested instant. It is the model that the element sets are fitted to, so it is the correct way to use them; a general purpose numerical integrator given the same elements would drift away from the published positions. Two branches exist and the propagator selects between them by orbital period. A satellite with a period below 225 minutes is propagated with SGP4, which models the secular effect of the Earth's oblateness and a drag term. A satellite at or above that period is propagated with SDP4, which adds the resonance and the luni-solar perturbations that dominate at that altitude. Inputs and outputs: - Elements are the mean elements from [`apsis_tle::TwoLineElement`]. Angles in the element set are in degrees and mean motion is in revolutions per day; this crate converts to radians and radians per minute internally. - The output is expressed in the True Equator Mean Equinox (TEME) frame, with position in kilometers and velocity in kilometers per second. TEME is the frame the model defines; converting it to an Earth-fixed frame requires the Earth rotation and the equation of the equinoxes and is not part of this crate. - Time is measured from the element set epoch, in minutes. Source: the algorithm follows Vallado et al., *Revisiting Spacetrack Report #3*, AIAA 2006-6753, 2006, and the revised implementation distributed with that paper. ``` use apsis_sgp4::{GravityModel, Satellite}; use apsis_tle::TwoLineElement; let text = concat!( "1 25544U 98067A 08264.51782528 -.00002182 00000-0 -11606-4 0 2927\r\n", "2 25544 51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.72125391563537\r\n", ); let element = TwoLineElement::parse(text).expect("sample is well formed"); let satellite = Satellite::from_element(&element, GravityModel::WGS72) .expect("sample elements are propagatable"); // Propagate to the epoch of the elements. let state = satellite.propagate_minutes(0.0).expect("epoch state exists"); // The position of a low Earth satellite is a few thousand kilometers // from the center of the Earth. assert!(state.position.norm() > 6_600.0); assert!(state.position.norm() < 7_200.0); ```

it does in the sequential form; the threads do not stop at the first such
minute, because a caller usually wants the whole track and will decide for
itself what a decay means.

Propagation is deterministic and depends only on the minutes, so the
result does not depend on how the work was split.

The gain depends on how much work the list holds, because starting the
threads costs a fixed amount that a short list cannot repay. A day at a
one minute step is fourteen hundred states and gains little; a month is
forty three thousand and gains several fold. A caller with many short
tracks is better served by the per satellite form below, which takes the
whole list in one call.

items.name: unkozai_mean_motion
items.signature: pub fn unkozai_mean_motion( mean_motion: f64, eccentricity: f64, inclination: f64, model: GravityModel, ) -> f64 {
items.doc:
Applies the Kozai to Brouwer mean motion correction.

The mean motion in an element set is a Kozai mean motion, which the
theory must convert to a Brouwer mean motion before use. The relation is

```text
n0 = n / (1 + 1.5 k2 (3 cos^2 i - 1) / (a^2 sqrt(1 - e^2)) / a^2)
```

written in the form used here as a fixed point iteration, because `a`
depends on `n0` through Kepler's third law. The iteration converges from
the unmodified mean motion in a few steps for every orbit that appears in
an element set.
Applies the Kozai to Brouwer mean motion correction.

The mean motion in an element set is a Kozai mean motion, which the
theory must convert to a Brouwer mean motion before use. Writing `no` for
the element set value and `xke` for the Kepler constant, the reference
implementation evaluates

```text
ak   = (xke / no)^(2/3)
d1   = 0.75 j2 (3 cos^2 i - 1) / (sqrt(1 - e^2) (1 - e^2))
del  = d1 / ak^2
adel = ak (1 - del^2 - del (1/3 + 134 del^2 / 81))
del  = d1 / adel^2
n0   = no / (1 + del)
```

The second evaluation of `del` uses `adel` rather than `ak`, which is
what makes the correction consistent with the semi-major axis implied by
the corrected mean motion.

Source: Vallado et al., *Revisiting Spacetrack Report #3*, AIAA
2006-6753, 2006.

crates.name: apsis-kepler
crates.summary: Keplerian orbital elements and two-body propagation. A Keplerian element set describes an orbit as an ellipse, a parabola, or a hyperbola with a fixed orientation in space. From the six elements and the gravitational parameter, this crate computes the position and velocity at any time under the two-body assumption, and converts in the other direction. The two-body model includes only the point mass gravity of the central body. It omits the oblateness of the Earth, drag, and third body perturbations, so it drifts from reality over time. It is the right model for analysing an orbit whose elements are already known, for example to find the radius at a true anomaly, and the wrong model for propagating a two-line element set, which is the job of `apsis-sgp4`. Angles are in radians. Lengths are kilometers and the gravitational parameter is in cubic kilometers per second squared, matching the rest of the orbit layer. ``` use apsis_kepler::{GravityParameter, KeplerianElements}; // A circular orbit at the Earth's equatorial radius has the speed // sqrt(mu / r), about 7.9 km/s. let elements = KeplerianElements { semi_major_axis: 6_378.137, eccentricity: 0.0, inclination: 0.0, right_ascension: 0.0, argument_of_perigee: 0.0, true_anomaly: 0.0, }; let state = elements.to_state(GravityParameter::WGS84).expect("valid elements"); assert!((state.velocity.norm() - 7.909).abs() < 0.01); ```

crates.name: apsis-ephemeris
crates.summary: Ephemeris sampling and interpolation. A propagator gives the state of a satellite at any instant, but calling it millions of times is wasteful when the result is only needed to draw a track or to search for a crossing. This crate records the state at a grid of times, called samples, and answers queries between them by interpolation. The two halves are deliberately independent: - [`Ephemeris`] is a table of times and states. It knows nothing about where the states came from, so a table propagated by SGP4, computed by two-body theory, or read from a file all work the same way. - [`Sampler`] fills a table by calling a function that produces a state from a time. In this workspace that function is normally `apsis_sgp4::Satellite::propagate_at`, but the sampler only requires a closure, so a test can use an analytic function. Interpolation is Hermite cubic, which uses both the position and the velocity at each end of an interval. Using the velocity is what makes it accurate: a cubic through two positions alone has no information about how fast the satellite is moving, while Hermite reconstruction matches the slope at both ends and so reproduces a smooth orbit far better for the same sample spacing. On a circular orbit the error is of order the fourth power of the step, so halving the step cuts the error about sixteen fold. Times are in seconds from an origin chosen by the caller, matching the rest of the orbit layer. Positions are in kilometers and velocities in kilometers per second. ``` use apsis_ephemeris::{Sample, Sampler}; use apsis_kepler::{GravityParameter, KeplerianElements}; // A circular orbit at the Earth's equatorial radius. let elements = KeplerianElements { semi_major_axis: 7_000.0, eccentricity: 0.0, inclination: 0.9, right_ascension: 0.0, argument_of_perigee: 0.0, true_anomaly: 0.0, }; let state_at = |seconds: f64| { let mean = 2.0 * core::f64::consts::PI * seconds / elements.period(GravityParameter::WGS84); let state = elements .with_mean_anomaly(mean) .to_state(GravityParameter::WGS84) .expect("the orbit is valid"); Sample::new(seconds, state.position, state.velocity) }; let sampler = Sampler::new(0.0, 600.0, 60.0); let ephemeris = sampler.sample(state_at).expect("the grid is usable"); assert_eq!(ephemeris.len(), 11); // A query between two samples is interpolated. let state = ephemeris.state_at(30.0).expect("the time is covered"); assert!(state.position.norm() > 6_900.0); ```

crates.name: apsis-maneuver
crates.summary: Impulsive and finite orbital maneuver models. A maneuver changes an orbit by applying thrust. The two models here are the two ends of the spectrum. An impulsive maneuver, [`Impulse`], applies a velocity change instantaneously, so the position is unchanged and only the velocity jumps. This is the model for a chemical burn, whose duration is short compared with the orbital period, and it is the model every textbook delta-v budget is written in. It is exact in the limit of zero burn time and the source of the closed form results for transfers between two orbits. A finite maneuver, [`FiniteBurn`], applies a constant acceleration over a duration, so the position drifts during the burn and the achieved velocity change is less than the thrust would give in free space when the thrust has to fight gravity. It is the model for an electric thruster, whose burn may last a large fraction of an orbit, and for any burn where the short duration approximation is not good enough. The two agree in the limit: a finite burn of acceleration `a` over a duration `t` delivers the impulse `a t`, so a [`FiniteBurn`] with a vanishing duration converges on the matching [`Impulse`]. The tests check that limit, which is what ties the two models together. The impulsive model also provides the classic two impulse transfer between two coplanar circular orbits, [`hohmann_transfer`], which is the reference every low thrust result is compared against. It gives the two burns and the total delta-v for a transfer between two circular orbits of given radii, together with the transfer time, the half period of the transfer ellipse. Conventions match the rest of the orbit layer: lengths are in kilometers, velocities in kilometers per second, and angles in radians. ``` use apsis_maneuver::{Impulse, hohmann_transfer}; use apsis_kepler::GravityParameter; use apsis_math::Vec3; // An impulsive burn straight along the velocity. let impulse = Impulse::new(Vec3::new(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)).expect("the change is usable"); assert!((impulse.magnitude() - 1.0).abs() < 1e-12); // The two burns that raise a circular orbit from 7000 to 8000 km. let transfer = hohmann_transfer(7_000.0, 8_000.0, GravityParameter::WGS84) .expect("the radii are usable"); assert!(transfer.first_burn > 0.0); assert!(transfer.total_delta_v() > 0.0); ```

A maneuver that applies a constant acceleration for a duration.

A finite burn is the model for a thruster that is on for long enough that
its duration cannot be ignored: an electric thruster, whose burn may last
a large fraction of an orbit, or any burn where the spacecraft moves
appreciably while thrusting.

The acceleration is held constant in an inertial frame chosen by the
caller. That is the simplification this model makes: a real thruster
fires along a body axis that rotates as the spacecraft turns to hold a
direction, and modelling that requires the attitude history, which is not
part of this crate.

so the integration is a fixed step fourth order Runge-Kutta, which is
accurate for the short arcs a burn occupies.

The achieved velocity change is measured against a coast of the same
duration, not against the initial velocity. That distinction matters:
gravity changes the velocity during the burn even with no thrust, so
the difference between the final and the initial velocity includes
the natural rotation of the velocity vector. Comparing against the
coast isolates the contribution of the thrust, which is what the
burn bought; it also makes the result converge on the nominal change
as the duration shrinks, which the difference from the initial
velocity would not.

Returns the state at the end of the burn together with the achieved
velocity change.

items.name: HohmannTransfer
items.doc:
A two impulse transfer between two coplanar circular orbits.

The transfer is the classic Hohmann maneuver: a burn onto an ellipse
whose perigee touches the lower orbit and whose apogee touches the upper
one, a coast for half the ellipse's period, and a second burn onto the
destination circle. It is the cheapest two impulse transfer between two
coplanar circular orbits in the impulsive model, which is why it is the
reference every other transfer is measured against.

The burns are signed along the direction of motion: a positive value
raises the orbit and a negative one lowers it, so the same type covers a
climb and a descent. The total is the sum of the magnitudes, which is the
quantity a propellant budget uses.

items.doc: Returns the velocity change of the first burn, unsigned.

items.name: second_burn_magnitude
items.doc: Returns the velocity change of the second burn, unsigned.

items.name: mean_radius
items.doc:
Returns the mean radius the transfer is symmetric about, in
kilometers.

This is the semi-major axis of the ellipse, which is the arithmetic
mean of the two orbit radii.

items.name: hohmann_transfer
items.signature: pub fn hohmann_transfer( from_radius: f64, to_radius: f64, parameter: GravityParameter, ) -> Result<HohmannTransfer, ManeuverError> {
items.doc:
Returns the two impulse transfer between two circular orbits.

The radii are in kilometers and must be finite and positive. The two may
be given in either order: a larger second radius is a climb and a smaller
one a descent.

Returns an error when a radius is not usable or when the two are equal,
because a transfer between an orbit and itself is not a maneuver and is
almost always a mistake in a plan.

The burns follow from the vis-viva equation. At the first radius the
circular speed is `sqrt(mu / r1)` and the speed on the transfer ellipse
is `sqrt(mu (2 / r1 - 1 / a))`, where `a` is the semi-major axis of the
ellipse, so the first burn is the difference. The second burn is the
difference between the circular speed at the destination and the speed on
the ellipse there, taken the other way round because the ellipse arrives
slower than the circle it must join. The coast time is half the period of
the ellipse.

An instantaneous change in velocity.

An impulse is a velocity change applied in zero time, so it changes the
velocity of a state but not its position. That is the model for a burn
short compared with the orbital period, and it is how a delta-v budget is
written.

The change is stored as a vector in the same frame as the state it will
be applied to, so the caller is responsible for expressing it in that
frame. The magnitude is the delta-v, the quantity a propellant budget is
measured in.

crates.summary: Orbital state facade that integrates the orbit layer. This crate is the single entry point to the orbit layer. It re-exports the element parsing, the analytical propagator, and the two-body model, and adds one type that ties them together. [`Orbit`] holds a satellite prepared for propagation together with the gravity model it was initialised against, and offers the conversions between the two ways of describing an orbit that the layer supports: - Mean elements propagated by SGP4, which is the model a two-line element set is written for and the only way to reproduce the published positions of a catalogued satellite. - Instantaneous Keplerian elements, which describe the osculating two-body orbit at one instant and are useful for inspection and for planning a maneuver. The two descriptions are not interchangeable. Propagating mean elements with the two-body model, or osculating elements with SGP4, gives a different and wrong answer; the conversions here are explicit about which direction they go. Two further operations are built on the propagation and exposed here because they need the same gravity parameter to stay consistent: - [`Orbit::sample_ephemeris`] records the track on a time grid so that it can be queried by interpolation instead of by propagation, which is what a coverage or access search wants. - [`Orbit::apply_burn`] applies a finite maneuver to the osculating state and returns the resulting elements, which is what a maneuver plan produces. ``` use apsis_orbit::{GravityModel, Orbit}; use apsis_tle::TwoLineElement; let text = concat!( "1 25544U 98067A 08264.51782528 -.00002182 00000-0 -11606-4 0 2927\r\n", "2 25544 51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.72125391563537\r\n", ); let element = TwoLineElement::parse(text).expect("sample is well formed"); let orbit = Orbit::from_element(&element, GravityModel::WGS72) .expect("sample elements are propagatable"); let state = orbit.propagate_minutes(60.0).expect("state exists"); assert!(state.speed() > 7.0); // The osculating elements at that instant. let osculating = orbit.osculating_elements(60.0).expect("state exists"); assert!(osculating.eccentricity < 0.01); ```

crates.summary: Constellation definition and instantiation. A constellation is a set of satellites described by a small number of parameters rather than as a list of individual orbits. This crate models two forms of construction that together cover the constellations in operational use: - A **Walker constellation**, in which satellites are spread evenly over a set of orbital planes that share an inclination and a semi-major axis, with a fixed phase relationship between adjacent planes. - A **custom constellation**, where each shell is described separately so that a design that does not follow the Walker pattern can still be instantiated. Both forms produce a list of [`KeplerianElements`] at a reference time, which the orbit layer can propagate. The constellations in use for satellite internet are Walker patterns at several altitudes, so the Walker constructor is the one most callers need. The Walker notation is written `i: t/p/f`, where `i` is the inclination in degrees, `t` the total number of satellites, `p` the number of planes, and `f` the phase factor. The satellites are placed so that `t / p` satellites share each plane and adjacent planes are offset in mean anomaly by `f * 360 / t` degrees. Source: the Walker notation and the phasing rule are the ones defined in Walker, J. G., *Circular Orbit Patterns Providing Continuous Whole Earth Coverage*, Royal Aircraft Establishment Technical Report 70211, 1970. ``` use apsis_constellation::{Constellation, WalkerPattern}; // A Walker 53 degree pattern with 24 satellites in 3 planes. let pattern = WalkerPattern { total_satellites: 24, planes: 3, phase_factor: 1, inclination: 53.0_f64.to_radians(), semi_major_axis: 6_878.137, }; let constellation = Constellation::walker(pattern, 0.0).expect("the pattern is consistent"); assert_eq!(constellation.satellites().len(), 24); ```

crates.summary: Ground coverage analysis. A satellite covers the part of the Earth's surface from which it can be seen above a minimum elevation angle. That part is a circle, called the footprint, whose size depends on the satellite altitude and on the elevation mask. This crate computes the footprint geometry, tests whether a ground point lies inside a footprint, and measures how much of a region is covered. The spherical model in [`geometry`](self) treats the Earth as a sphere. That is accurate enough for constellation design, where the quantities wanted are the footprint radius to a few parts in ten thousand and the number of satellites in view. The exact line-of-sight test in [`line_of_sight`] uses the actual positions, so it accounts for the flattening and for a ground point above the ellipsoid. The geometry of the satellite, the ground point, and the centre of the Earth is a triangle. Its three angles are the elevation at the ground point, the nadir angle at the satellite, and the central angle at the centre, and they sum to a right angle: ```text elevation + nadir + central = 90 degrees ``` Source: the relations used here are the standard satellite geometry, as given for example in Vallado, D. A., *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics and Applications*, 4th edition, microcosm Press, 2013, section 5.3. ``` use apsis_coverage::{footprint_central_angle, slant_range}; // A satellite at 550 km altitude sees to about fifteen degrees of // central angle at a ten degree elevation mask, which is a footprint // radius of some 1665 km along the surface. let central = footprint_central_angle(6_928.137, 6_378.137, 10.0_f64.to_radians()) .expect("valid geometry"); assert!((central.to_degrees() - 14.96).abs() < 0.01); let range = slant_range(6_928.137, 6_378.137, 10.0_f64.to_radians()) .expect("valid geometry"); assert!((range - 1_815.65).abs() < 0.01); ```

satellite, the ground point, and the centre of the Earth,

crates.summary: Ground station access windows. A satellite is accessible from a ground station during the intervals when it rises above the station's elevation mask. Each such interval is a pass, or access window, and the sequence of windows over a period is the access schedule. This crate finds those windows from a propagated orbit and reports their start, end, duration, and the geometry at their peak. The windows are found by sampling the elevation angle at a fixed step and refining each crossing where the elevation passes the mask. The elevation is evaluated from the satellite position in the Earth-fixed frame, so the caller supplies the transformation from the orbit frame. items.signature: pub fn find(&self, samples: &[OrbitSample]) -> Result<PassSummary, AccessError> {
items.doc:
Finds the access windows in an ordered sequence of samples.

The samples must be ordered by time and cover the interval of
interest. The finder assumes the elevation is continuous between
samples, so the step must be short enough that the satellite does not
rise and set within one step. A low Earth satellite is above a
ten degree mask for several minutes, so a step of a minute or less
satisfies that.

The crossing times are found by interpolating the satellite position
linearly between the two samples that straddle the crossing. The
chord between two samples departs from the true arc by an amount of
the second order in the step, so a ten second step gives a crossing
accurate to about a tenth of a second and a one second step to about
a millisecond. Use [`AccessFinder::find_with`] when the propagator is
available and the crossing is wanted to the full tolerance.

A pass that is already in progress at the first sample is reported
with its rise at the first sample time, and one still in progress at
the last sample is reported with its set at the last sample time.
That convention means the pass is clipped to the interval searched
rather than extrapolated beyond it.

Returns an error when the settings are not usable, when the sample
sequence has fewer than two entries, or when a sample is not usable.

crates.name: apsis-topology
crates.summary: Time-varying network topology. A satellite network is not a single graph. The set of usable links changes as the satellites move, so the network is a sequence of graphs indexed by time, and this crate provides the data structures for that sequence. The model is deliberately simple. A [`Topology`] is a graph with a fixed set of nodes, which are satellites or ground stations, and a set of edges that may be present or absent. A [`TopologySeries`] is a sequence of topologies at increasing times, together with the interval each one applies to. The series is a step function: a topology holds from its own time until the time of the next entry. That is the standard discrete time model for a time-varying graph, and it is what routing over the series expects. Edges carry a cost as well as their presence, so that a routing algorithm has something to minimise. The cost is a plain number, so a caller may put a delay, a hop count, or anything else in it, as long as the routing algorithm and the cost agree on the meaning. ``` use apsis_topology::{Topology, TopologySample, TopologySeries}; // Two satellites linked to each other. let mut topology = Topology::new(2); topology.add_edge(0, 1, 1.0).expect("the nodes exist"); assert!(topology.has_edge(0, 1)); let series = TopologySeries::new(vec![TopologySample::new(0.0, topology)]) .expect("the series is not empty"); assert_eq!(series.len(), 1); assert!(series.topology_at(0.0).expect("a topology exists").has_edge(0, 1)); ```

crates.name: apsis-isl
crates.summary: Inter-satellite link geometry and visibility. Two satellites can form a link when the straight line between them does not pass through the Earth. This crate decides that condition, gives the geometry a link budget needs, and reports the range and the angles at which each satellite must point. The blocking test is whether the line segment between the two positions has any point inside the body. For a spherical body that is a perpendicular distance test, which is exact and cheap, so it is the one used here. An optical link adds a second condition: the Sun must not be within the field of view of either terminal, because the background would swamp the signal. That is a separate test, offered as [`sun_blocks_link`], which takes the direction to the Sun. Lengths are in kilometers and angles in radians. The positions are in a frame in which the Earth is a sphere of the given radius, which for link geometry is the same frame the orbit layer produces. ``` use apsis_isl::{LinkGeometry, link_geometry, mutual_visibility}; use apsis_math::Vec3; // Two satellites on the same side of the Earth see each other. let first = Vec3::new(6_928.137, 0.0, 0.0); let second = Vec3::new(6_868.137, 2_500.0, 0.0); assert_eq!(mutual_visibility(first, second, 6_378.137), Some(true)); // Two satellites on opposite sides do not. let opposite = Vec3::new(-6_928.137, 0.0, 0.0); assert_eq!(mutual_visibility(first, opposite, 6_378.137), Some(false)); ```

items.doc:
Returns the visibility of every ordered pair of positions, in order.

The result is row major: the entry at `row * positions.len() + column` is
the visibility from `positions[row]` to `positions[column]`. A satellite is
always visible to itself, which is the caller's cue to skip the diagonal.

A pair whose test is undefined, because a position is not finite or the
body radius is not positive, yields `false`.

same order. The pairs are independent, so splitting the flat index space

the work is divided.

The gain from threading is modest here and shrinks as the matrix shrinks.
A single visibility test is a few nanoseconds, so the cost of starting the
threads is only repaid by a large matrix: on a sixteen core machine a few
hundred satellites already gain, while a few dozen lose. The sequential
form is the better choice for a small shell, and this one exists for the
large ones where the quadratic sweep dominates.

The test is the angle between the link direction and the direction to the

Sun is in the beam and the link cannot be used.

The field of view is given as a half angle in radians, which is the
acceptance cone of the telescope. A typical optical terminal has a half

crates.summary: Routing over time-varying satellite topologies. The topology of a satellite network changes as the satellites move, so a route is only valid over an interval. This crate computes least cost routes through a [`Topology`] and reports the route together with the time it remains valid. Two forms of routing are provided: - [`shortest_path`] finds the least cost route through the topology in force at one instant. - [`route_over_series`] finds a route that is valid for a whole interval, by taking the intersection of the topologies across that interval. crates.name: apsis-handover
crates.summary: Handover decision logic for mobile terminals. A terminal that can be served by more than one satellite must choose one, and it must change its choice when the current server becomes unsuitable. This crate makes that decision. It does not compute access windows, which belong to the access layer; it takes a list of candidate satellites with their quality and decides whether to hand over. Two effects oppose each other and both must be in the policy: - **Handing over too late** loses the link. If the current server drops below the terminal's minimum, the link fails before the switch happens. - **Handing over too often** wastes capacity and time. Each handover costs signalling and interrupts the data flow, so a terminal that switches on every small fluctuation performs poorly even though each individual choice looked better. The policy therefore has three parts: a threshold at which the current server is considered unusable, a margin by which a candidate must beat the current server before it is worth switching to, and a minimum time between handovers. The margin is what suppresses oscillation, and it is the hysteresis of the decision. Source: the threshold, margin, and dwell time structure is the one used for handover in cellular and satellite networks, as described for example in ITU-R Recommendation M.1184 on the technical and operational characteristics of mobile satellite systems, and in the general treatment of handover hysteresis in mobile radio. ``` use apsis_handover::{Candidate, HandoverPolicy, HandoverDecision, decide}; let policy = HandoverPolicy { minimum_quality: 0.2, handover_margin: 0.1, minimum_dwell_seconds: 5.0, }; // The current server is fine and the alternative is only slightly // better, so nothing happens. let candidates = [ Candidate::new(1, 0.8, 100.0), Candidate::new(2, 0.85, 90.0), ]; let decision = decide(&policy, Some(1), &candidates).expect("valid input"); assert_eq!(decision, HandoverDecision::Stay); ```

items.doc:
Returns the decision implied by the policy, without a dwell time.

This is the form to use when the terminal makes an independent decision
at each instant and the caller tracks the history itself. Use
[`decide_with_history`] when the dwell time must be enforced.

The rules, in the order they are applied:

1. With no current server, acquire the best candidate, or drop when none
   meets the minimum quality.
2. When the current server is not among the candidates, it has become
   unavailable, so switch to the best candidate or drop when none meets
   the minimum quality.
3. When the current server is below the minimum quality, abandon it for
   the best candidate, or drop when none meets the minimum quality.
4. Otherwise stay, unless a candidate exceeds the current server's
   quality by more than the margin.

Returns an error when the candidates or the policy are not usable.

crates.name: apsis-mesh
crates.summary: Mesh connectivity abstractions. A satellite mesh is a set of terminals that reach each other through links, some of which are satellite links and some of which are ground links. This crate provides the abstractions that a mesh application needs on top of a topology: which terminals can reach which others, how many independent ways there are to do so, and which links are critical. The three questions this crate answers: - **Reachability**: the set of terminals reachable from a given one. - **Redundancy**: how many independent paths join two terminals, which is the number of links that can fail independently. This is the edge-connectivity of the graph, by Menger's theorem. - **Criticality**: the links whose removal would separate the mesh, which are the ones a network operator must protect. The redundancy computation is exact for the small graphs a satellite mesh presents. It uses the edge version of Menger's theorem, computing the connectivity from a sequence of maximum flow problems, each of unit capacity. Source: Menger's theorem, and the reduction of edge connectivity to maximum flow, as given in Cormen et al., *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd edition, MIT Press, 2009, chapter 26. ``` use apsis_mesh::Mesh; use apsis_topology::Topology; // Three terminals in a ring, so each pair has two independent paths. let mut topology = Topology::new(3); topology.add_bidirectional_edge(0, 1, 1.0).expect("the nodes exist"); topology.add_bidirectional_edge(1, 2, 1.0).expect("the nodes exist"); topology.add_bidirectional_edge(2, 0, 1.0).expect("the nodes exist"); let mesh = Mesh::new(topology); assert!(mesh.is_connected()); assert_eq!(mesh.edge_connectivity(0, 1), Some(2)); ```

items.doc:

Two paths are independent when they share no edge. By Menger's theorem
that number is the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects the
two nodes, so it is the number of link failures the connection survives.

The value is computed as a maximum flow of unit capacity between the two
nodes, using the Edmonds-Karp variant of the Ford-Fulkerson method, which
augments along a shortest path at each step. For the small graphs of a
satellite mesh this is fast, and it is exact.

Returns `Some(0)` when no path exists, and `None` when either node is out
of range or the two nodes are the same, for which the question is not
defined.

which nodes finish, and a second search over the reversed edges, taking
the nodes in reverse finishing order, emits the components.

Source: Kosaraju's algorithm as described in Cormen et al.,
*Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd edition, MIT Press, 2009, chapter 22.

crates.summary: Core radio frequency primitives. This crate holds the quantities that the rest of the radio frequency layer is written in: power, gain, and the decibel scale that both are usually quoted on, together with the two relations that every link calculation starts from, the wavelength of a frequency and the free space path loss. Units are SI throughout. Power is in watts, frequency in hertz, distance in meters, and temperature in kelvin. Decibel values are power ratios, computed as ten times the base ten logarithm of the ratio. Two conventions are worth stating because they are easy to mix up: - A decibel is a ratio between two powers. A gain expressed in `dBi` is a ratio to an isotropic radiator and one in `dBd` is a ratio to a half wave dipole, which is 2.15 dB more directive than an isotropic radiator. [`Gain`] carries the ratio and both named forms. - The free space path loss increases with frequency as well as with distance, because both the effective aperture of a fixed gain antenna and the solid angle it subtends shrink as the wavelength shortens. ``` use apsis_rf::{Power, wavelength}; // A noise power of -204 dBW is about 4e-21 W. let noise = Power::from_dbw(-204.0).expect("the reading is finite"); assert!(noise.watts() > 0.0); // A one meter wavelength corresponds to a frequency of 299.792 MHz. let lambda = wavelength(299_792_458.0).expect("the frequency is positive"); assert!((lambda - 1.0).abs() < 1e-12); ```

The type stores the decibel value rather than the ratio, because a chain
of gains and losses is then a sum, which is both faster and less prone to

items.signature: pub fn free_space_path_loss(distance: f64, frequency: f64) -> Option<Decibel> {
items.doc:
Returns the free space path loss between two isotropic antennas, as a
ratio in decibels.

The ratio is positive, so it represents a loss: the received power is the
transmitted power divided by this ratio. The relation is

```text
L = (4 pi d / lambda)^2
```

which is the spreading loss of a spherical wave over a distance `d`
combined with the effective aperture of an isotropic receive antenna.

The loss grows with frequency at a fixed distance, because the effective
aperture of the receive antenna falls as the square of the wavelength.

The distance must be positive. A zero distance is not a case this
expression covers: the ratio would be zero, which is infinite attenuation
in decibels, and the underlying far field assumption does not hold.

Returns `None` when the distance is not positive, or when either argument
is not finite.

items.signature: pub fn free_space_received_ratio( distance: f64, frequency: f64, transmitter: Gain, receiver: Gain, ) -> Option<Decibel> {
items.doc:
Returns the received power ratio between two antennas in free space.

The received power is the transmitted power multiplied by the two antenna
gains and divided by the free space path loss, which in decibels is the
sum

```text
P_r / P_t = G_t G_r / L
```

The result is the ratio in decibels, so a positive value means the
receive antenna collects more than was transmitted, which happens when

crates.name: apsis-antenna
crates.summary: Antenna radiation patterns and gain models. An antenna does not radiate equally in every direction. This crate models how the gain varies with angle for the two shapes that appear in almost every satellite link: a parabolic reflector, whose beam is a narrow pencil, and an idealised element with a broad pattern. Three beam width conventions are used in practice and they are not interchangeable: - The half power beam width is the angle between the two directions where the gain has fallen to half its peak, which is three decibels down. - The null to null beam width is the angle between the first two zeros on either side of the main lobe. It is roughly twice the half power width for a uniformly illuminated aperture. - The first sidelobe level is the peak gain outside the main lobe. For a uniformly illuminated circular aperture it is about minus 17.6 dB. Every function here takes or returns angles in radians and gains as [`apsis_rf::Gain`], so a result can be fed straight into a link budget. Sources: - Parabolic aperture gain: `G = eta (pi D / lambda)^2`, where `eta` is the aperture efficiency, typically between 0.55 and 0.70 for a well adjusted dish. - Half power beam width of a circular aperture: `theta = k lambda / D` with `k` about 1.02 for uniform illumination and close to 1.2 for typical illumination tapers. - The co-polar reference pattern of a simple Earth station antenna, which falls as the square of the off-axis angle down to a sidelobe floor. This is the form used by ITU-R Recommendation S.465 to bound interference from one satellite system into another. ``` use apsis_antenna::ParabolicAperture; // A three meter dish at twelve gigahertz has a peak gain near 50 dBi. let dish = ParabolicAperture { diameter: 3.0, efficiency: 0.65, }; let peak = dish.peak_gain(0.025).expect("valid wavelength"); assert!(peak.dbi().expect("positive") > 45.0); assert!(peak.dbi().expect("positive") < 50.0); ```

A parabolic reflector described by its diameter and aperture efficiency.

The aperture efficiency collects every loss between the power delivered
to the feed and the power that leaves the aperture as a uniform plane
wave: illumination taper, spillover, blockage by the feed and its
supports, and surface error. A well adjusted dish reaches 0.65 to 0.70,
and a small or simply built one is nearer 0.55.

which follows from the effective area through

Returns `None` for an invalid aperture or wavelength.

A tapered illumination reduces the sidelobes at the cost of a wider

1.02 for uniform illumination to about 1.2 for the taper that
minimises sidelobes. A value of 1.15 is representative of a
well designed dish.

Returns `None` for an invalid aperture or wavelength.

items.name: beam_width

items.doc:
Returns the half power beam width of a circular aperture, in radians.

The relation is `theta = k lambda / D`, where `k` depends on how the
aperture is illuminated. Uniform illumination gives the narrowest beam,
with `k` about 1.02, and the taper that suppresses sidelobes gives the
widest, with `k` about 1.2.

The result is the full width between the two three decibel points, not
the half width. It is a small angle approximation, so the caller should
confirm that the resulting width is small compared to a radian.

Returns `None` when the diameter or wavelength is not positive, or when
`k` is not positive.

items.name: floor_angle
items.signature: pub fn floor_angle(beam_width: f64, floor_db: f64) -> Option<f64> {
items.doc:
Returns the angle at which the squared angle law of
[`off_axis_attenuation`](crate::off_axis_attenuation) reaches the
sidelobe floor.

Beyond this angle the model holds the gain at the floor rather than
letting it fall without bound. The angle follows from setting the
attenuation `12 (theta / theta_0)^2` equal to the floor, which gives
`theta = theta_0 sqrt(floor / 12)`.

Returns `None` when the beam width or floor is not positive and finite.

items.name: off_axis_attenuation
items.signature: pub fn off_axis_attenuation( peak: Gain, beam_width: f64, off_axis_angle: f64, floor_db: f64, ) -> Option<Decibel> {
items.doc:
Returns the gain of an antenna at an angle from boresight, given a peak
gain and a half power beam width.

This is the squared angle model that several interference assessments
use, expressed in terms of the half power beam width so that any antenna
can be described by the two numbers a link budget has to hand. In
decibels,

```text
G(theta) = G_peak - min(12 (theta / theta_0)^2, G_floor)
```

where `theta_0` is the half power beam width and `G_floor` is the
sidelobe level to fall to, in decibels below the peak. The squared angle
law comes from the first term of the Airy pattern of a uniformly
illuminated aperture, which is a good approximation down to the first
sidelobe.

The coefficient twelve is chosen so that the attenuation reaches three
decibels at `theta_0 / 2`, which is the definition of the half power beam
width. A pattern taken from a recommendation should be used in place of
this one where the recommendation applies: see
[`reference_pattern_gain`](crate::reference_pattern_gain) for the ITU-R
S.465 pattern, which differs from this model in the main lobe and also in
the shape of its sidelobe region.

Returns `None` when the peak gain has no decibel form, or when the beam
width or floor is not positive and finite.

items.name: mask_gain
items.signature: pub fn mask_gain(diameter_over_wavelength: f64, off_axis_angle: f64) -> Option<f64> {
items.doc:
Returns the gain that an antenna is required not to exceed at an angle
from boresight, in decibels relative to an isotropic radiator.

This is the reference pattern of the Radio Regulations Appendix 8, used
to check whether an Earth station meets the off-axis emission limits that
protect neighbouring satellites. The pattern is piecewise:

```text
for  D/lambda >= 100:
  G = 29 - 25 log10(theta)            for 1   <= theta < 36 degrees
  G = -10                             for 36  <= theta <= 180 degrees
for  D/lambda <  100:
  G = 32 - 25 log10(theta)            for 1   <= theta < 48 degrees
  G = -10                             for 48  <= theta <= 180 degrees
  G = 32 - 25 log10(48)               for theta < 1 degree
```

The angle is in radians and the diameter to wavelength ratio decides
which branch applies, because a small antenna has a broader main lobe
and therefore a wider range over which the pattern must be controlled.

This function returns the limit, that is the largest gain permitted. An
antenna is compliant when its actual off-axis gain is at or below it.

Returns `None` when the angle is negative, when the ratio is not
positive, or when the angle is not finite.

Source: ITU, *Radio Regulations*, Appendix 8, which reproduces the
reference pattern of ITU-R Recommendation S.465.

crates.name: apsis-doppler
crates.summary: Doppler shift computation. A satellite and a ground station move relative to each other, so the frequency that arrives at the receiver differs from the frequency that left the transmitter. This crate computes that shift from the relative velocity. Two effects are present and they are separate. The classical shift is proportional to the range rate divided by the speed of light, and it is what a Doppler tracker compensates. The relativistic time dilation between the two clocks is a second order correction that is far smaller for orbital velocities, and it is offered separately so that a caller can include it when the application needs it. The sign convention used here is that a positive range rate, meaning the two terminals are moving apart, produces a negative shift and therefore a lower received frequency. This matches the everyday observation that a receding source sounds lower. ``` use apsis_doppler::{DopplerShift, range_rate_from_velocity}; use apsis_math::Vec3; // A satellite at the first axis moving away along it. let range_rate = range_rate_from_velocity( Vec3::new(7_000_000.0, 0.0, 0.0), Vec3::new(1_000.0, 0.0, 0.0), ); assert_eq!(range_rate, Some(1_000.0)); let shift = DopplerShift::from_range_rate(12.0e9, 1_000.0).expect("valid"); assert!(shift.shifted_frequency() < 12.0e9); ```

items.name: range_rate_from_velocity
items.signature: pub fn range_rate_from_velocity(relative_position: Vec3, relative_velocity: Vec3) -> Option<f64> {
items.doc:
Returns the range rate between two terminals, in meters per second.

The range rate is the component of the relative velocity along the line
between the terminals. A positive value means the separation is
increasing.

The first argument is the position of the remote terminal relative to the
local one, so that its magnitude is the separation. The second is the
velocity of the remote terminal relative to the local one. Both are in
SI units.

Returns `None` when the separation is zero, because no line of sight is
defined there, or when either argument is not finite.

items.name: classical_shift
items.signature: pub fn classical_shift(carrier_frequency: f64, range_rate: f64) -> Option<f64> {
items.doc:
Returns the classical Doppler shift of a frequency for a range rate, in
hertz.

The relation is

```text
delta f = -f_0 (v_r / c)
```

where `v_r` is the range rate, positive when receding. The shift is
negative for a receding terminal, so the received frequency is lower than
the transmitted one.

The magnitude of the shift is small compared to the carrier: a range rate
of 7 km/s at 12 GHz gives about 280 kHz, which is two parts in a hundred
thousand. The caller must therefore treat the frequency as a double, and
the shifted frequency is returned separately rather than by adding a
small shift to a large number.

Returns `None` when the frequency is not positive and finite, or when the
range rate is not finite.

items.name: relativistic_doppler_factor
items.doc:
Returns the relativistic Doppler factor for a range rate.

The factor is `sqrt((1 - beta) / (1 + beta))` with `beta = v_r / c`.
Multiplying the transmitted frequency by it gives the received frequency
to all orders in `beta`, so it is not a small correction to the classical
shift but the quantity the classical shift approximates.

Its expansion is `1 - beta + beta^2 / 2 - ...`. The first two terms are
the classical result, which is `1 - beta` to within a factor that is
itself second order, and the remaining terms are the difference between
the two treatments. For a satellite at orbital velocity, `beta` is about
`2.3e-5` and the second order term is about `2.7e-10` of the carrier, so
the two agree to a few parts in ten to the tenth.

Returns `None` when the range rate is not finite, or when its magnitude
reaches the speed of light, where the expression has no real value.

items.doc:
A Doppler shift applied to a carrier.

The type carries the carrier frequency and the range rate, so the

available without ambiguity about which sign convention was used.

Returns the shift including the relativistic clock correction, in
hertz.

The received frequency is the carrier multiplied by the relativistic
factor, so the shift is `f_0 (factor - 1)`.

This is not the classical shift plus a small correction: the factor
already contains the first order term, and its expansion is
`1 - beta + beta^2 / 2 - ...`, whose leading term is exactly the
classical shift. The classical value is the first order
approximation to this one, and the two differ only by the second and
higher order terms, of order `beta^2`, which for a satellite is a few
parts in ten to the tenth of the carrier.

The factor is evaluated first and the carrier multiplied afterwards,
because the difference from one is tiny and would lose precision if
the shift were added to the carrier before the correction.

Returns `None` when the range rate reaches the speed of light.

The result lies in `[0, pi]`.

The result is returned as a positive magnitude. Returns `None` when the
